hints: Recall the work-energy principle: because the block travels at constant speed, there is no change in kinetic energy.
The total work supplied by the crane must equal the increase in gravitational potential energy plus the work done to overcome resistance.
Calculate the potential energy gain using $\Delta PE = mgh$ with $m = 600\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $h = 15\text{ m}$, then add the $10\,000\text{ J}$ of resistance work.
walkthrough:
Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy of the block:
$$\Delta PE = mgh = 600 \times 10 \times 15 = 90\,000\text{ J}$$

Compute the total work done by the crane by adding the work done against resistance:
$$\text{Total work done} = \Delta PE + W_{\text{resistance}} = 90\,000 + 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ J}$$

ai_rubric.Applying the Work\u2013Energy Principle: Calculates gravitational potential energy gain $600(10)(15) = 90\,000\text{ J}$ and finds total work done $90\,000 + 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ J}$.

teacher_walkthrough:
State the work-energy principle for vertical motion at constant speed:
$$\text{Work done by crane} = \Delta KE + \Delta PE + W_{\text{resistance}}$$
Since the block moves at constant speed, the change in kinetic energy is zero:
$$\Delta KE = 0$$
Therefore, the crane only needs to supply the energy to increase potential energy and overcome resistance:
$$\text{Work done by crane} = \Delta PE + W_{\text{resistance}}$$

Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained using $\Delta PE = mgh$:
- Mass of the block: $m = 600\text{ kg}$
- Acceleration due to gravity: $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$
- Vertical height: $h = 15\text{ m}$
$$\Delta PE = (600)(10)(15)$$
Multiply the terms:
$$\Delta PE = 6000 \times 15 = 90\,000\text{ J}$$

Add the work required to overcome resistance to the potential energy gain:
$$\text{Total work done} = 90\,000 + 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ J}$$
Thus, the total work done by the crane is $100\,000\text{ J}$.

hints: Recall the fundamental definition of average power: $P = \frac{W}{t}$, where $W$ is work done and $t$ is time.
Convert the power from kilowatts to watts ($12.5\text{ kW} = 12\,500\text{ W}$) and use the total work done $W = 100\,000\text{ J}$ from part (a).
Rearrange $12\,500 = \frac{100\,000}{t}$ to solve for the time $t$.
walkthrough:
Set up the relationship between work done, power, and time:
$$P = \frac{W}{t}$$
$$12\,500 = \frac{100\,000}{t}$$

Solve for the time of motion $t$:
$$t = \frac{100\,000}{12\,500} = 8\text{ s}$$

ai_rubric.Using Power and Resistance Relationships: Applies $P = W/t$ with $P = 12\,500\text{ W}$ and $W = 100\,000\text{ J}$, and solves to obtain $t = 8\text{ s}$.

teacher_walkthrough:
State the formula relating average power, work done, and elapsed time:
$$P = \frac{W}{t}$$
Identify the given quantities:
- Power: $P = 12.5\text{ kW} = 12.5 \times 1000 = 12\,500\text{ W}$
- Work done: $W = 100\,000\text{ J}$ (from part (a))

Substitute these values into the power equation:
$$12\,500 = \frac{100\,000}{t}$$

Multiply both sides by $t$:
$$12\,500t = 100\,000$$
Divide both sides by $12\,500$:
$$t = \frac{100\,000}{12\,500}$$
Simplify the division:
$$t = \frac{1000}{125} = 8\text{ s}$$
Thus, the total time for which the block is in motion is $8\text{ s}$.
